config.title: Lifting State Up

intro.title: Lifting State Up
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple temperature converter app that allows users to input a temperature in either Celsius or Fahrenheit and see it instantly converted in the other unit. You'll learn the core React concept of 'lifting state up,' which involves moving shared state to the closest common ancestor component to keep multiple components in sync. The main technologies and constructs you'll use include React components, state management with the useState hook, and event handlers to pass data between components. This approach helps avoid duplicated state and ensures your app's data flows in a single, predictable direction.
intro.usecase: Lifting state up is essential when multiple UI components need to stay synchronized with the same data. In e-commerce sites, product filters (price range, category, ratings) often control a separate product listing component—both need access to the same filter state. Dashboard applications use this pattern when date range selectors update multiple charts and data tables simultaneously. Form wizards also rely on lifted state to share user input across different steps while maintaining a single source of truth.

objectives: Construct a parent component that manages shared state for multiple child components
Implement state lifting by passing callback functions from parent to child components
Manipulate shared state through child components using lifted callback handlers
Configure controlled components by binding their values to lifted state
Update UI synchronization across multiple components through centralized state management
Initialize a React application with properly structured parent-child state relationships
Render multiple independent components that interact through a common lifted state source

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns JSX containing a <div> with no content inside.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is created and returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named exactly 'App' and returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you defined a function named App returning a <div>.

steps.title: Initialize shared state in App
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use useState to create a state variable named 'temperature' with an initial value of 20.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value and destructure the returned array into temperature and setTemperature.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a temperature state variable initialized to 20, ready to be shared with child components.
successCriteria: The App component contains a useState call that creates a temperature state variable with initial value 20.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using useState to create a variable named 'temperature' with initial value 20 inside the App component.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the App component, use useState to create a state variable called 'temperature' starting at 20.

steps.title: Create TemperatureDisplay component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TemperatureDisplay that takes a 'temperature' prop and returns a paragraph showing the temperature value.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function called TemperatureDisplay that accepts props and returns JSX with the temperature value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TemperatureDisplay component is defined that accepts a temperature prop and renders it in a paragraph.
successCriteria: TemperatureDisplay component is created with a 'temperature' prop and returns a paragraph element containing the temperature value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but make sure it accepts a 'temperature' prop and renders it in a paragraph.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a function named TemperatureDisplay that takes a temperature prop and returns a paragraph with that value.

steps.title: Display temperature in TemperatureDisplay
steps.instruction: Inside the TemperatureDisplay component, return JSX that shows the temperature value passed via props. The component should display the temperature value inside a paragraph element.
steps.hint: Use the props parameter to access the temperature value, then return a paragraph element containing that value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureDisplay component will render a paragraph showing the temperature value it receives through props.
successCriteria: TemperatureDisplay returns JSX with a paragraph element containing the temperature value from props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your TemperatureDisplay component returns a paragraph element containing the temperature value from props.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TemperatureDisplay component should return JSX that displays the temperature value passed via props.

steps.title: Create TemperatureControls component
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named TemperatureControls that takes a prop called 'onTemperatureChange' and returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a component with a single parameter for props, then return null inside the function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a TemperatureControls component defined that accepts onTemperatureChange as a prop and returns null.
successCriteria: TemperatureControls component is created with a parameter for onTemperatureChange and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named TemperatureControls and accepts onTemperatureChange as a prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a functional component named TemperatureControls with a parameter for onTemperatureChange.

steps.title: Add increment and decrement buttons to TemperatureControls
steps.instruction: Inside the TemperatureControls component, return a JSX fragment containing two buttons: one labeled 'Increase' and one labeled 'Decrease'.
steps.hint: You can use a fragment (<>...</>) or a <div> to wrap the buttons. Each button should have a text label.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureControls component now returns two buttons: 'Increase' and 'Decrease'.
successCriteria: TemperatureControls returns JSX containing two <button> elements with the labels 'Increase' and 'Decrease'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have exactly two buttons with the correct labels.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that your TemperatureControls component returns two button elements with the specified labels.

steps.title: Define temperature change handler in App
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, define a function named handleTemperatureChange that takes a single parameter 'change' and updates the temperature state by adding that change value to the current temperature.
steps.hint: You can create the function using either function declaration or arrow function syntax. Inside the function, use the setTemperature function to update the state based on the current temperature plus the change parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now contains a handleTemperatureChange function that can update the temperature state by a specified amount.
successCriteria: The handleTemperatureChange function is defined in the App component, takes a 'change' parameter, and calls setTemperature with the updated value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes a 'change' parameter and properly updates the temperature state using setTemperature.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named handleTemperatureChange that updates the temperature state based on the change parameter.

steps.title: Wire TemperatureControls to the handler
steps.instruction: Pass the handleTemperatureChange function as a prop named onTemperatureChange to the TemperatureControls component in App's return statement.
steps.hint: In the App component's return statement, add the onTemperatureChange prop to the TemperatureControls component and pass the handleTemperatureChange function as its value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureControls component will receive the handler function as a prop, enabling the buttons to update the shared temperature state.
successCriteria: TemperatureControls component is rendered with an onTemperatureChange prop that passes the handleTemperatureChange function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're passing the handleTemperatureChange function as the value of the onTemperatureChange prop to TemperatureControls.
steps.feedbackWrong: In the App component's return statement, add the onTemperatureChange prop to TemperatureControls and pass handleTemperatureChange as its value.

steps.title: Render child components in App with shared state
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, render the TemperatureDisplay and TemperatureControls components, passing the temperature state and handleTemperatureChange function as props.
steps.hint: Remember to pass props to child components using the same prop names they expect. TemperatureDisplay should receive temperature, and TemperatureControls should receive handleTemperatureChange.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will render both child components, passing the shared state and handler as props to enable lifting state up.
successCriteria: TemperatureDisplay and TemperatureControls are rendered in App's return statement with temperature and handleTemperatureChange passed as props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're rendering both TemperatureDisplay and TemperatureControls, and passing the correct props to each.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're rendering both child components in App's return statement and passing the temperature state to TemperatureDisplay and handleTemperatureChange to TemperatureControls.
